reception.text: The Morning Oregonian's Washington bureau put the signing on page one and called it "record time in creating forest reserves."
Short wire items in La Grande and Salem papers reported the signing without comment or objection.
reception.source: La Grande Morning Observer, February 7, 1904, p. 1; Weekly Oregon Statesman, February 9, 1904, p. 4

political_impact.text: Oregon's Senator Fulton and Representative Williamson called on Roosevelt the morning he signed and urged him to act promptly.

legacy.text: The reserve was broken up in 1906: part went into the new Blue Mountains reserve, the rest returned to the public domain, and the Baker City name was dropped.
legacy.source: 34 Stat. 3194; Forest Service, Establishment and Modification of National Forest Boundaries (1959)

related.note: The Blue Mountains proclamation took in part of the Baker City reserve and ended it as a separate reserve.

uncertain: The General Land Office estimated the reserve at 52,480 acres, one section more than a count of the sections in the proclamation's own description; the reason is not known.

reception.text: Before the signing, a Washington dispatch reprinted across California tied the larger Warner Mountain proposal to the indicted Hyde–Benson land ring, which had bought barren land inside its lines to trade for timber scrip.
reception.source: Humboldt Times, February 25, 1904; Mariposa Gazette, March 19, 1904

political_impact.text: The reserve answered an Alturas mass meeting that asked, with no reported dissent, for a permanent Modoc reserve to protect the streams feeding the Pit River valleys, and a petition from more than two hundred farmers and stock raisers.

political_impact.text: Senator Weldon B. Heyburn of Idaho, the reserves' most persistent critic in Congress, was writing to the White House about forest reserves by September 1904.
political_impact.source: Pinchot to Loeb, September 12, 1904 (TR Center o46805)

political_impact.text: Where there was friction it was local and economic: ranchers, sheepmen and timber operators often saw new reserves as a lock-up of range and timber, while irrigators in places like Modoc County asked for them.

reception.text: California papers carried thirty-six items on the Warner Mountain reserve from 1903 to 1905, across twenty-one titles.

legacy.text: The Transfer Act moved the reserves to the Department of Agriculture; Pinchot's bureau became the Forest Service that July, and the reserves became national forests in 1907.
The Colorado reserves of 1904 live on within the White River, Grand Mesa and Pike national forests.
legacy.source: Forest Service, Establishment and Modification of National Forest Boundaries (1959)
